summary: Defines a MIB module of textual conventions for MPLS management information, so that other MPLS MIB modules can import them instead of defining their own. It was updated by RFC 7274.

plainLanguage.summary: Several dashboards need the same kinds of labels. This defines them once so everyone can reuse them.

questions: what is a textual convention in a mib
what are the reserved mpls label values
what is an mpls lsp id
subtitle: A shared dictionary of data types that MPLS management MIB modules import instead of each inventing their own.

tldr.problem: Every MIB module that manages MPLS needs the same kinds of values, such as labels, bit rates, tunnel indexes and LSP identifiers, and would otherwise define its own incompatible versions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines one SMIv2 module, MPLS-TC-STD-MIB, containing only TEXTUAL-CONVENTIONs, rooted at mplsStdMIB under { transmission 166 }, for other MPLS MIB modules to import.
tldr.outcome: MPLS MIB modules can share consistent types for labels, LSP and tunnel identifiers, and enumerations. The RFC was later updated by RFC 7274.

today: RFC 3811 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 7274. The text itself states no later usage.

sections.title: Purpose and Framework
sections.content:
RFC 3811 defines a MIB module of Textual Conventions (TCs) for Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) networks. MIB modules that manage MPLS networks are meant to import these TCs rather than define their own representations.

The module follows the Internet-Standard Management Framework. Managed objects live in a virtual information store called the Management Information Base (MIB), generally accessed through SNMP, and objects are defined with the Structure of Management Information. This module is compliant with SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.
sections.plainLanguage: A textual convention is a named kind of value, like "a bit rate" or "a label". This document is the list of names that all MPLS management tools agree to use.

sections.title: The MPLS-TC-STD-MIB Module
sections.content:
The module is named MPLS-TC-STD-MIB. Its identity is mplsTCStdMIB, placed at { mplsStdMIB 1 }, with mplsStdMIB itself at { transmission 166 }. The only revision is dated June 3, 2004, described as the initial version published as part of RFC 3811. It imports MODULE-IDENTITY, Unsigned32, Integer32 and transmission from SNMPv2-SMI and TEXTUAL-CONVENTION from SNMPv2-TC.

The module defines no managed objects, only types. Those types fall into a few groups: rates and sizes, labels and label handling, identifiers for LSRs and LSPs, enumerations about how labels and LSPs are managed, tunnel indexes, and addresses of tunnel hops.
sections.plainLanguage: The module is a numbered shelf in a big library of network definitions. Each type is a labeled box on that shelf.

sections.title: Rates, Sizes and Labels
sections.content:
MplsBitRate is an Unsigned32 in units of 1,000 bits per second, rounded to the nearest 1,000. A value of 0 means the traffic is considered best effort. MplsBurstSize is the number of octets of MPLS data a stream may send back-to-back without concern for policing, with 0 meaning the implementation does not support burst size.

MplsLabel represents an MPLS label and is an Unsigned32 whose meaning depends on the kind of label. A label in an MPLS shim header is a 20-bit number carried in 4 octets, with bits 0-19 holding the label and bits 20-31 required to be zero. The description quotes the reserved values from RFC 3032, and says Frame Relay labels can be 10 or 23 bits depending on the DLCI field size. For ATM labels, the lower 16 bits are the VCI, the next 12 bits are the VPI and the remaining bits MUST be zero. A GMPLS label has a value greater than 2^24-1.

MplsAtmVcIdentifier holds an ATM VCI or VPI/VCI in the range 32 to 65535. VCI values 0 to 31 are reserved for other uses by the ITU and ATM Forum and MUST NOT be used, and the value 32 can only be used for the Control VC. Breaking these rules should result in an inconsistentValue error.
sections.plainLanguage: A bit rate is how fast, counted in thousands. A label is a small tag stuck on a packet that tells routers where to send it, and some tag numbers are saved for special jobs.

sections.title: LSR, LSP and Tunnel Identifiers
sections.content:
An LDP identifier, MplsLdpIdentifier, is a six octet value. The first four octets identify the Label Switching Router (LSR) and must be globally unique, such as a 32-bit router ID, and the last two octets identify a label space within that LSR. MplsLsrIdentifier is just the first 4 bytes of it.

MplsLSPID is a unique identifier within an MPLS network for each Label Switched Path (LSP), assigned at the head end. It is an octet string of size 2 or 6. For RSVP-TE it is a 16-bit (2 byte) identifier, and for CR-LDP it is 6 bytes, where the first two bytes carry the CR-LSPID and the remaining 4 carry the Router ID. MplsExtendedTunnelId identifies an MPLS tunnel and may represent an IPv4 address of the ingress or egress LSR.

For tunnels, MplsTunnelIndex is a value from 0 to 65535 that should match the RSVP Tunnel ID. MplsTunnelInstanceIndex uses 0 for the configured tunnel interface, values from 1 to 65535 for signaled or backup tunnel LSP instances, and values above 65535 for FRR detour instances. MplsPathIndex indexes a path from 1 upward, and MplsPathIndexOrZero allows 0 to mean that no path is in use. MplsTunnelAffinity is a 32-bit include-any, include-all or exclude-all constraint.
sections.plainLanguage: Every router needs a name tag, and every path through the network needs a ticket number. These types say how long those names and numbers are and what they are made of.

sections.title: Enumerations for Modes and Types
sections.content:
Several TCs are small enumerations. MplsLabelDistributionMethod is downstreamOnDemand(1) or downstreamUnsolicited(2), and each interface on an LSR operates in one of them. MplsRetentionMode is conservative(1), which keeps only label mappings that will be used to forward packets, or liberal(2), which keeps all advertised mappings. MplsLdpLabelType is generic(1), atm(2) or frameRelay(3).

MplsLspType says how an LSP relates to the router: unknown(1), terminatingLsp(2), originatingLsp(3) or crossConnectingLsp(4). MplsOwner records which local management subsystem created an object, from unknown(1) through other(2), snmp(3), ldp(4), crldp(5) and rsvpTe(6) to policyAgent(7). An object created by any of them MAY be modified or destroyed by the same or a different one.
sections.plainLanguage: These are multiple-choice answers. For each question, such as who made this path, there is a short fixed list of allowed answers.

sections.title: Traffic Engineering Hop Addresses
sections.content:
A Traffic Engineered tunnel hop can be named in several ways. TeHopAddressType picks the kind: unknown(0), ipv4(1), ipv6(2), asnumber(3), unnum(4) or lspid(5). TeHopAddress is an octet string of size 0 to 32 and is always interpreted in the context of its type object. An address can be a concrete host or interface, an abstract node such as an IPv4 prefix shorter than 32, or an Autonomous System.

The two objects must stay consistent. Setting a TeHopAddress that does not match its type must fail with an inconsistentValue error, and the type and address must be changed together. TeHopAddressType SHOULD NOT be sub-typed in object definitions, to allow future extensions. TeHopAddressAS is a four-octet AS number in network byte order, where a two-octet AS number has the two most significant octets set to zero. TeHopAddressUnnum is a four-octet unnumbered interface index.
sections.plainLanguage: A hop address is like a stop on a bus route. It can be a single house, a whole street, or a whole town, and the type field says which one you mean.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The module defines no management objects, so the RFC says meaningful security considerations can only be written in the MIB modules that define them, and this document has no impact on the security of the Internet.

IANA assigned mplsStdMIB under { transmission 166 }, because 166 is the ifType for mpls(166). Future MPLS standards track MIB modules should be rooted under that subtree, and new assignments can only be made via a Standards Action as specified in RFC 2434. IANA also assigned { mplsStdMIB 1 } to MPLS-TC-STD-MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: This is only a list of names, so it cannot be hacked by itself. The number registry makes sure nobody else uses the same shelf.

viz.caption: RESERVED MPLS LABEL VALUES QUOTED FROM RFC 3032 (RFC 3811, MplsLabel)

items.label: IPv4 Explicit NULL
items.desc: Only legal at the bottom of the label stack; pop the stack and forward on the IPv4 header.

items.label: Router Alert
items.desc: Legal anywhere except the bottom of the stack; delivered to a local software module.

items.label: IPv6 Explicit NULL
items.desc: Only legal at the bottom of the label stack; pop the stack and forward on the IPv6 header.

items.label: Implicit NULL
items.desc: Assigned and distributed by an LSR but never appears in the encapsulation; the LSR pops instead.

items.label: unknown
items.desc: The creating component cannot be determined.

items.label: other
items.desc: Known but not listed, for example a command line interface.

items.label: ldp
items.desc: Configured through the Label Distribution Protocol.

items.label: policyAgent
items.desc: Configured by a policy agent, perhaps with one of the above.
